title: Misc. bug: Performance regression: CUDA sparse flash attention decode 1.6x slower (b11047 -> b11062)
body:
### Name and Version

```
version: 0.4.1-dev (build 11062, commit 3cf03257f)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Compared against build 11047, commit `b23701f77`.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

ggml (CUDA backend)

### Command line

```bash
test-backend-ops perf -b CUDA0 -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT
```

Built with:

```
-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON -DGGML_CUDA_GRAPHS=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`FLASH_ATTN_EXT` on the sparse path costs 64 percent more at batch one after
[#28770](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28770), median over the 11 sparse configurations
`test-backend-ops` generates. The worst is 113 percent. Dense shapes are untouched. RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell
Workstation Edition, sm_120, driver 615.71.09, CUDA 13.4.

Run the command above at `3cf03257f` and at `b23701f77` and compare the configurations whose `n_kv_max` is not 0.
Use console output, since `--output csv` drops the timings.

Every sparse configuration, `us/run`:

| hsk | nh  | kv    | n_kv_max | b11047 | b11062 | delta |
| --- | --- | ----- | -------- | ------ | ------ | ----- |
| 512 | 1   | 49152 | 2048     | 25.80  | 55.01  | +113% |
| 512 | 1   | 32768 | 512      | 18.29  | 37.58  | +106% |
| 576 | 1   | 49152 | 2048     | 29.17  | 58.83  | +102% |
| 576 | 1   | 32768 | 512      | 21.78  | 41.60  | +91%  |
| 512 | 1   | 16384 | 512      | 13.58  | 23.27  | +71%  |
| 256 | 2   | 32768 | 2048     | 22.55  | 36.97  | +64%  |
| 576 | 1   | 16384 | 512      | 17.12  | 27.14  | +59%  |
| 256 | 2   | 16384 | 2048     | 15.03  | 22.53  | +50%  |
| 512 | 1   | 4096  | 512      | 10.21  | 12.64  | +24%  |
| 576 | 1   | 4096  | 512      | 13.59  | 16.18  | +19%  |
| 256 | 2   | 4096  | 2048     | 16.45  | 11.81  | -28%  |

Dense shapes over the same range moved 0.1 percent median on 58 decode configurations and 0.3 percent on 29 batched
ones. Nothing outside the sparse path changed.

**Where the time goes.** Dividing the added time by the mask width gives a constant, within each head size and across
a twelve-fold range of `kv`:

| hsk | nh  | kv    | n_kv_max | added us | ns per mask column |
| --- | --- | ----- | -------- | -------- | ------------------ |
| 512 | 1   | 4096  | 512      | +2.43    | 0.593              |
| 512 | 1   | 16384 | 512      | +9.69    | 0.591              |
| 512 | 1   | 32768 | 512      | +19.29   | 0.589              |
| 512 | 1   | 49152 | 2048     | +29.21   | 0.594              |
| 576 | 1   | 4096  | 512      | +2.59    | 0.632              |
| 576 | 1   | 16384 | 512      | +10.02   | 0.612              |
| 576 | 1   | 32768 | 512      | +19.82   | 0.605              |
| 576 | 1   | 49152 | 2048     | +29.66   | 0.603              |

The cost tracks `kv` and ignores `n_kv_max`, including across the pair at `n_kv_max` 512 and 2048 that read 0.589 and
0.594. The attention kernel's work is bounded by `n_kv_max`, so it cannot produce this. The mask scan reads exactly
`kv` columns per list, so it can. I have not profiled the two kernels separately, so this is inference from the
scaling rather than a direct attribution.

It points at the new inner loop in `flash_attn_mask_to_sparse_indices`:

```c
for (int q = 0; q < q1 - q0 && !selected; ++q) {
    selected = i < ne30 && isfinite(__half2float(mask[q*s31 + i]));
}
```

where it used to be a single test. The trip count is a runtime value and the exit is data dependent, so the
`#pragma unroll` over `values_per_lane` around it no longer yields straight line code. At `ncols1 == 1` the body
always runs once and the union reduces to the old single-query test, so specialising that case, or templating the
kernel on `ncols1`, would recover it without touching the batched path the PR was written for.

The one configuration that improved, `kv=4096` at `n_kv_max=2048`, fits the same reading. The new per-list count
bounding `kb0_stop` is a real win, and at that shape it is larger than the scan cost.

**Scope.** `test-backend-ops` only generates sparse configurations at `nb=1`, so this says nothing about the batched
sparse path. The models reaching it are the ones calling `ggml_flash_attn_ext_set_n_kv_max`, currently `qwen4exp` and
`deepseek4`. A server decoding at batch one, meaning one slot and no draft model, sits on the regressed shape for
every token.

### First Bad Commit

`3cf03257f` (#28770, "CUDA: enable sparse fa for qwen4").

15 commits separate `b23701f77` from `3cf03257f`, and only `3cf03257f` touches `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/` at all. The rest
are Metal, Hexagon, server, chat and UI changes.

I measured [#28536](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28536) separately, as the other CUDA flash attention
change in the neighbourhood. It costs 0.7 percent on these same configurations, so it is not involved.

title: Feature Request: Add dependency cooldown for pip packages
body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

To protect against supply-chain attacks, add a pip dependency cooldown similar to our npm cooldown (see https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26711).

### Motivation

There's been a surge in supply-chain attacks.

It'll often go like this: An attacker hacks a maintainer's account or gets the maintainer to transfer package ownership to them. The attacker pushes a package update containing malicious code. Once a developer installs the package, their machine is compromised. Examples: [1a](https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised), [1b](https://socket.dev/blog/axios-maintainer-confirms-social-engineering-behind-npm-compromise), [2](https://socket.dev/blog/tinycolor-supply-chain-attack-affects-40-packages), [3](https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack).

Usually, these instances are detected by automated scanning tools within a few hours. However, a malicious package often still remains online on package registries for a few hours. During that time, if someone installs the package, their machine is compromised.

We can reduce exposure to these attacks by waiting a few days to install newly-published packages.

### Possible Implementation

_No response_

title: Feature Request: expose last-token hidden state during normal inference
body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Currently llama-server --embedding --pooling last can expose the last-token representation, but this puts the server into embedding-only mode.

It would be useful to expose the same representation while running a model in normal generative mode.

For example:

llama-server -m qwen3-8b.gguf -c 8192

could serve both:

/v1/chat/completions
/v1/representations

where /v1/representations returns the last-token hidden state from the normal forward pass.

This would allow lightweight models/heads to query a general-purpose LLM without requiring a separate embedding instance or switching the model into --embedding mode.

A concrete use case is [Contrastive Language Models (CLM)](https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM), which uses Qwen3-8B with last-token representations and a small downstream head.

Ideally, when generation is already running, the representation should be obtained from the same forward pass rather than performing another inference.



### Motivation

This would make hidden-state extraction a per-request capability of a normal generative model rather than a server-wide embedding mode.

### Possible Implementation

llama-server -m qwen3-8b.gguf -c 8192

could serve both:

/v1/chat/completions
/v1/representations

title: Feature Request: Support Prism PQ2_0 (GGML type 142) and PTQ1_0 (type 143) used by Ternary-Bonsai-2
body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description


## Summary

Public GGUFs for [prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf) use two **new** GGML tensor types that stock `ggml-org/llama.cpp` does not know:

| Name | Tensor type ID | Role |
|------|---------------:|------|
| `PQ2_0` | **142** | 2-bit slots for ternary g128 (`{-1,0,+1}` + FP16 group scale) |
| `PTQ1_0` | **143** | dense trit packing of the same ternary g128 weights |

These are **not** upstream `Q1_0` (type 41) and **not** upstream `Q2_0` (type 42, group 64). They were given high IDs so they can coexist with those types.

Stock `llama-cli` rejects them as unknown types. If a loader treats an unknown type as `Q2_0`, Prism’s card says the result is **garbage** (no Hadamard activation transform).

This is a request to either:

1. **Upstream** `PQ2_0` / `PTQ1_0` (parse + dequant + matmul, including the Hadamard path), or
2. **Reject loudly** with the type name, and document that these files need the Prism fork until they land.

I am not affiliated with Prism ML. I hit this while importing the public GGUFs (also via Ollama `create`, which vendors llama.cpp and fails the same way).

## Public files (Apache 2.0)

Repo: https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf

| File | Size (bytes) | `general.file_type` | Dominant tensor type |
|------|-------------:|--------------------:|---------------------:|
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf` | 7,206,168,928 | 141 | **142** (`PQ2_0`) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` | 5,946,648,928 | 143 | **143** (`PTQ1_0`) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-F16.gguf` | 53,808,408,928 | F16 | 1 (not the issue) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-mmproj-Q8_0.gguf` | 629,246,976 | Q8_0 | 8 (loads; vision only) |

Architecture metadata: `qwen35`. Example tensor: `output.weight` / `token_embd.weight` shape `[5120, 248320]`, type 142 or 143.

Verified SHA256 (HF LFS):

- PQ2_0: `3907dc1658db1f78a9826bf8d5bcb8dc65db0d466388937af57f2294fae62ec1`
- PTQ1_0: `53107f530aa52eb00912263ab1ee29bd199261c87cd7b4ad4ca1318c1fe33ee3`

## How this differs from formats that already work

| Format | Typical file | Type ID | Mainline llama.cpp | Notes |
|--------|--------------|--------:|:------------------:|-------|
| 1-bit Bonsai `Q1_0` | `prism-ml/Bonsai-27B-gguf` `Bonsai-27B-Q1_0.gguf` | 41 | Yes (e.g. [#20048](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/20048) / follow-ups) | This is what Ollama listings like `*:bonsai-27b-q1_0` run |
| Ternary `Q2_0` g64 | `*-Q2_0_g64.gguf` | 42 | Yes (CPU/Metal/Vulkan; CUDA tracked separately) | Official upstream ternary packing |
| Fork ternary `Q2_0` g128 | `*-Q2_0.gguf` (Bonsai 1) | 42, **different block size** | No (same id, wrong layout) | [Bonsai-demo ternary status](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo#upstream-status-for-ternary) |
| **Bonsai 2 `PQ2_0` / `PTQ1_0`** | files above | **142 / 143** | **No** | New IDs + Hadamard-rotated ternary |

Bonsai 2 is a new checkpoint (Qwen3.8-27B lineage, hybrid attention, 262K context), not a requant of Bonsai-27B `Q1_0`.

## What Prism’s fork already names

From [PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp) `ggml/include/ggml.h` (`prism` branch):

```c
GGML_TYPE_Q1_0    = 41,
GGML_TYPE_Q2_0    = 42,
// Prism-private Q2_0 at group size 128 (upstream Q2_0 is group 64). High id so it
// slots above upstream types; type_traits is sized to COUNT (143) with 43..141 unused.
GGML_TYPE_PQ2_0   = 142,
GGML_TYPE_PTQ1_0  = 143, // Prism-private ternary, group 128
GGML_TYPE_COUNT   = 144,
```

The same header also defines `GGML_HINT_SRC0_IS_HADAMARD`. The [HF card](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf) says weights are stored after a blockwise Hadamard (block 1024); the runtime must apply the matching transform to activations or **refuse to load**. Registering a block size without that path is not enough.

Prism’s own demo README still lists `PQ2_0` as “planned / nothing yet” for the *previous* Ternary-Bonsai-27B drop. Bonsai 2 has already shipped files with types 142/143.

Reference implementation: https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp  
Demo / pinned binaries: https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo

## Reproduction (stock llama.cpp)

```bash
hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf \
  Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf \
  --local-dir .

# latest ggml-org/llama.cpp release binary
./llama-cli -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf -p "ping" -n 16
```

**Expected:** model loads, or a clear `unknown type 142 (PQ2_0)` error.

**Actual (stock):** unknown type / load failure. Downstream Ollama 0.33.2 `ollama create` reports `Error: tensor "output.weight" size overflow` because its GGUF parser returns type size 0 for 142/143.

Same result for `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` (type 143).

`Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-F16.gguf` is a standard F16 GGUF (~50.1 GiB) and is not the format users are meant to deploy.

## Packing (from Prism’s card + fork comments)

- Ternary g128: each weight in `{-1, 0, +1}`, one FP16 scale per 128 weights (~1.72 bits/weight including a small set of higher-precision tensors).
- `PTQ1_0`: dense trits, ~1.75 bpw, ~5.95 GB language model.
- `PQ2_0`: one trit in a 2-bit slot, ~2.13 bpw, ~7.21 GB; this is the pack Prism reports on Apple Silicon.
- Group size **128** (not upstream `Q2_0` group 64, not `TQ1_0`/`TQ2_0` group 256).

I do not have a public spec for the exact `block_pq2_0` / `block_ptq1_0` C layouts in this issue; those live in the Prism fork (`ggml-common.h` / quant kernels). Happy to help test a PR against the HF files above.

## Ask

1. Is upstream interested in `PQ2_0` / `PTQ1_0` as first-class types (similar to how `Q1_0` and `Q2_0` g64 landed)?
2. If yes, what is the preferred split (CPU dequant first, then Metal/CUDA/Vulkan)?
3. If not in the near term, would you accept a loader error that names types 142/143 so apps do not confuse them with `Q2_0`?

Related upstream work: [Q2_0 g64](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24448), [Q1_0](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/20048). I did not find an existing issue for types 142/143 / Ternary-Bonsai-2.

## Environment

- OS: macOS (Darwin 25)
- Tried: stock Ollama 0.33.2 (llama.cpp vendor); Ollama 0.34.2 source still has no type 142/143 sizes
- Files: HF `prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf` as of 2026-09-17

title: Feature Request: export/import slot state over http
body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Add new routes to export/import a slot over the http api.

### Motivation

A proxy like https://github.com/kokleong98/llama-proxy-cache or https://gitlab.com/inqode/ai-proxy that sits in front of multiple llama.cpp instances can route requests to different llama.cpp instances.

If requests from a longer session are routed to different backends on each request, the KV cache of each instance can not be used effectively. Multiple llama.cpp instances will occupy slots for the same session (could probably be mitigated by using "/slots/{slot}?action=save|restore" - but would require disk write/read on the inference machine). Also on each switch of a session from one backend to another, parts of the KV will have to be recomputed.

### Possible Implementation

Add two routes: `GET /slots/{SLOT}/state` and `PUT /slots/{SLOT}/state`.

These routes could use the same binary format that `POST /slots/{SLOT}?action=save` and `POST /slots/{SLOT}?action=load` are using to persist a slot to disk.

- `GET /slots/{SLOT}/state` will return a stream of the slot state
- `PUT /slots/{SLOT}/state` will accept a stream of the slot state

title: Eval bug: Vulkan/MoltenVK + AMD discrete GPU: ErrorDeviceLost with the default 4 server slots and prompts above ~70 tokens; --parallel 1 fixes it
body:
### Name and Version

version: 0.4.1-dev (build 1, commit 5836771) built with AppleClang 17.0.0.17000604 for Darwin x86_64

### Operating systems

Mac

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

Intel Core i9-12900F · 48 GB RAM · x86_64
AMD Radeon RX 6800 XT, 16 GB VRAM (RDNA2)
macOS 15.8 (24H23) · MoltenVK 1.4.2 · Vulkan 1.4.357
Built with -DGGML_METAL=OFF -DGGML_VULKAN=ON

ggml_vulkan: 0 = AMD Radeon RX 6800 XT (MoltenVK) | uma: 0 | fp16: 1 | bf16: 0 | fp4: 0 | warp size: 32 | shared memory: 65536 | int dot: 0 | matrix cores: none

### Models

Primary repro: Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M
Also observed with: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B / 14B-Instruct-Q4_K_M, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q4_K_M

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` crashes with `decode() failed: vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost` and triggers a macOS GPU driver reset (``Kernel_<timestamp>.gpuRestart``, visible as a screen flicker on both monitors; repeated occurrences eventually froze the display and required a hard power-off).

The trigger is the **interaction of two factors**:

1. The server's default `n_parallel = -1` → **4 slots + `kv_unified = true`** (`common/arg.cpp:1400`, `tools/server/server.cpp:154-157`)
2. A prompt above roughly **70 tokens**

**With `--parallel 1` the exact same prompt works reliably.**

`llama-bench` never reproduces it — it runs a single sequence, which is why `pp512` passes while a 75-token server prompt fails.

Possibly related to #17989 (`--parallel 1` reportedly still initializing 4 slots in some paths); on this build `--parallel 1` does produce `n_slots = 1` in the log.

### Steps to reproduce

```
llama-server -m Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 -c 4096
```

Then POST a `/v1/chat/completions` request whose prompt exceeds ~70 tokens. Fails on most attempts. Adding `--parallel 1` to the same command makes it reliable.

### Crossed controls

Same model, same machine, same session:

| Configuration | Prompt | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `--parallel 1` | 188 tokens | OK — 172 tokens generated, coherent (3/3) |
| `--parallel 4` (default) | 188 tokens | **FAIL** — ErrorDeviceLost + GPU reset |
| `--parallel 4` (default) | 51 tokens | OK (12/12 across the session) |

Threshold sweep with 4 slots, prompt sizes as reported by the server's own tokenizer:

| Prompt tokens | Result |
|---:|---|
| 50 | OK |
| 65 | OK |
| ~75 | **FAIL** |

### Hypotheses ruled out, each with a crossed control

- **Not context size** — fails at `-c 1024`, `-c 2048` and `-c 4096` alike; `-c 2048` with a short prompt succeeds.
- **Not generation length** — 128 / 256 / 512 `max_tokens` all pass with short prompts.
- **Not batch size** — `llama-bench` and `llama-server` share identical defaults (`n_batch 2048`, `n_ubatch 512`).
- **Not flash attention** — `-fa off` removes the `resolve_fused_ops: ... Flash Attention is assigned to device CPU` warning from the log and the failure persists.
- **Not a poisoned GPU/driver state** — a successful run happens 90 seconds after a failure + GPU reset, in the very configuration that had just failed.
- **Not model size or architecture** — reproduced with `llama` (8B) and `qwen2`.

### Secondary finding: silent output corruption

Two cases returned syntactically valid responses containing a **single repeated token** (normal `finish_reason`, normal token counts) instead of crashing:

- `Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q4_K_M` with the default 4 slots — 700 tokens, **1 distinct word**. With `--parallel 1` the same model returns correct output and passes a 13-case functional test suite.
- `Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct-Q4_K_M` **even with `--parallel 1`** — 250 tokens, 1 distinct word, including a U+FFFD character. The same model on CPU (`-ngl 0`) returns correct code and passes all 13 cases; `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B` (same architecture, 4.36 GB) is correct on GPU.

This matters because it is silent: without inspecting the content, the response looks like a normal completion. Possibly related to #20104.

### Note on severity

A GPU driver reset on this platform is visible to the user (screen flicker) and, when repeated, can hang the desktop. On Linux/RADV an over-allocation typically fails cleanly instead.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. First observed on 5836771.

### Relevant log output

srv    load_model: initializing, n_slots = 4, n_ctx_slot = 4096, kv_unified = 'true'
resolve_fused_ops: layer 0 is assigned to device Vulkan0 but Flash Attention is assigned to device CPU (usually due to missing support)

{"error":{"code":500,"message":"decode() failed: vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost","type":"server_error"}}

A matching Kernel_<timestamp>.gpuRestart report is written to /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/ on each failure.

Video input on Windows hangs in two different ways depending on where the MP4 MOOV atom is located. Both appear to be in the ffmpeg/ffprobe subprocess pipe handling in `tools/mtmd/mtmd-helper.cpp` (`mtmd_helper_video`). This extends #24394 (silent zero-frame failure on Linux) with Windows repro data — on Windows it hangs rather than failing silently.

**Case 1: MOOV atom at end of file (default ffmpeg output)**

`probe()` succeeds (ffprobe has to read the entire piped input to find the moov, so it fully drains stdin and exits cleanly). The ffmpeg decode step then produces zero frames:

```
0.24.617.771 D start_ffmpeg: launching: ffmpeg -nostdin -i cache:pipe:0 -vf fps=4.000000 -f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 pipe:1 -loglevel error
0.24.622.579 D start_ffmpeg: subprocess_create ret=0 proc_alive=1
0.24.622.583 D start_ffmpeg: starting feeder thread for 1194147-byte buffer
0.24.622.649 D read_next_frame: reading frame 0, expecting 2764800 bytes (720x1280)
0.24.668.259 D read_next_frame: fread returned 0 after 0/2764800 bytes (ferror=0)
0.24.668.268 D add_text: <|turn>system ...
0.24.668.306 D add_text: Video:
0.24.668.319 D add_text: Tell me about this video<turn|>
```

The prompt is assembled with the bare `Video:` text and no frames, and then llama-cli hangs (no generation, no error).

**Case 2: MOOV atom at front (`-movflags +faststart`)**

After remuxing the same file with `ffmpeg -i test.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart test_fast.mp4`, the hang moves *earlier*, into `probe()` itself. The log stops here and never prints the probe result line:

```
0.28.766.262 D res  add_waiting_: add task 0 to waiting list. current waiting = 0 (before add)
0.28.766.269 D que    post: new task, id = 0, front = 0
0.28.767.532 D probe: launching: ffprobe -v quiet -show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,duration -select_streams v:0 -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 pipe:0
(hangs indefinitely)
```

**Isolation: ffprobe itself behaves correctly on the same file**

Running the exact probe command manually with a real pipe (cmd.exe, binary-safe):

```
C:\Users\Ben>cmd /c "type C:\Users\Ben\Videos\test_fast.mp4 | ffprobe -v quiet -show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,duration -select_streams v:0 -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 pipe:0"
width=720
height=1280
r_frame_rate=30/1
duration=7.050391
nb_frames=211
The process tried to write to a nonexistent pipe.
```

ffprobe prints the metadata and exits promptly. Because the moov is at the front, it stops reading stdin early; the writer (`type`) gets the expected broken-pipe error and terminates. So the deadlock is in how `mtmd_helper_video` handles this early-exit case on Windows: the feeder thread is blocked in `fwrite()` on the child's stdin while the main thread is blocked in `fgets()` on the child's stdout, and neither unblocks when ffprobe stops reading / exits.

**Minor side issue** while debugging: the `probe()` debug line prints `fps_target` and a not-yet-assigned `info.n_frames`, e.g. `probe: 720x1280 fps=4.00 duration=7.02s n_frames=0` for a 30 fps / 211-frame video — `info.n_frames` is assigned on the line *after* the `LOG_DBG`, and `fps` here is the sampling target, not the source fps. Made the logs confusing to interpret.

Test video: 720x1280, H.264, 7.05 s, 30 fps, ~1.2 MB. Happy to provide the file or more verbose logs if useful.

Video input is new in #24269 (b9577); also reproduces after the #24316 refactor.

title: RPC client: RPC_STATUS_ASSERT in ggml_backend_rpc_buffer_get_tensor() aborts entire process on any RPC failure, instead of returning an error
body:
## Description

`ggml_backend_rpc_buffer_get_tensor()` (ggml/src/ggml-rpc/ggml-rpc.cpp, ~line 491 in our build) ends with:

```cpp
bool status = send_rpc_cmd(ctx->sock, RPC_CMD_GET_TENSOR, &request, sizeof(request), data, size);
RPC_STATUS_ASSERT(status);
```

If the GET_TENSOR RPC call fails for any reason, a network hiccup, or the remote server correctly rejecting an invalid/stale tensor reference via its own validation, e.g. the `buffer == nullptr && data != nullptr` check in `rpc_server::create_node()`, `RPC_STATUS_ASSERT` hard-aborts the entire client process (SIGABRT) instead of propagating an error up the call stack. In a multi-node RPC cluster serving a large model, this takes down the entire inference server, not just the one failed tensor fetch.

## Our environment

- 3-node RPC cluster: one orchestrator (primary llama-server, --rpc host1:50052,host2:50052) plus two rpc-server backends, serving Qwen3-235B-A22B (Q4_K_M GGUF) over a CX7 RDMA fabric
- Build: commit 3a3edc9ac (~b9704)
- Recurring crash, same signature every time, 10 occurrences over about 17 hours of use:

```
ggml_backend_rpc_buffer_get_tensor() [aborts here]
  ← ggml_backend_tensor_copy()
  ← ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async()
  ← llama_context::graph_compute()
  ← llama_kv_cache::update()
  ← llama_kv_cache_context::apply()
  ← llama_context::memory_update()
  ← llama_context::decode()
Main process exited, code=dumped, status=6/ABRT
```

## What we've tried

1. Disabled CUDA graph capture (GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1) on the theory this was the llama.cpp CUDA-graph-cache regression from #20315, crashed again with identical signature, GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS confirmed active in the process environment. Ruled out.
2. Reduced --parallel 4 to 1 on the theory that llama_kv_cache::update()'s cross-stream copy path (which only runs with --parallel greater than 1, per llama-kv-cache.cpp) was triggering an invalid RPC fetch during a cross-slot KV-cache copy. This reduced crash frequency but did not eliminate it, 3 more identical crashes occurred afterward with --parallel 1 confirmed active in the running process.

## Root cause (as far as we can tell)

Whatever originally causes a GET_TENSOR request to fail (still likely something in the slot-reassignment/cross-stream-copy path, possibly a timing/staleness issue against the remote server's tensor table) doesn't need to be a fatal condition on its own, RPC_STATUS_ASSERT turns any failed RPC call into a full process abort. We haven't identified why the underlying RPC call fails in the first place, but regardless of that cause, we don't think a failed GET_TENSOR should be able to kill the whole server.

## Suggested fix

Have ggml_backend_rpc_buffer_get_tensor() (and likely the sibling set_tensor/cpy_tensor RPC client functions, which have the same RPC_STATUS_ASSERT pattern) handle a failed RPC call gracefully, log an error and fail that specific tensor operation, rather than aborting the process. Happy to test a patch against our cluster if useful.

title: Feature Request: server: add option to concatenate prompts on /completion endpoint
body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

I propose to add a JSON argument `concat_instead_of_batch` to this endpoint. No existing clients would be affected because the default behavior of the endpoint is kept consistent.

### Motivation

-- Primary Use Case --

Jinja templating does not break apart control tokens in user inputs because the entire prompt stays in string form until user input is already mixed with template format. This is a limitation of Jinja, so I try to pretokenize user input and reimplement formatting myself in python (see attached files, which already makes use of the proof-of-concept on my fork).

[backend_gemma_4_llama_server.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30276497/backend_gemma_4_llama_server.py)
[session_structure.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30276496/session_structure.py)

However, this requires an endpoint that accepts a mix of token ID integers and multimodal data. Does the `POST /completion` endpoint not already do it? This is discussed in the next subsection.

-- Current Absence of Proposed Feature --

As of v10075 (on which proof-of-concept is implemented, see below) and v10096 (latest as of submitting this issue), the non-OpenAI `POST /completion` endpoint of `llama-server` interprets a mixed array in the `prompt` argument as a set of independent jobs instead of a single prompt to be sequentially concatenated. This subtlety has tripped up both Claude [(shared chat)](https://claude.ai/share/f9c80253-ccd5-4ad7-af2a-f2eaacd39511) and ChatGPT [(shared chat)](https://chatgpt.com/share/6a60ebfb-f324-83ea-8195-fddf3f9c9d73) as well as my friend Kaetemi.

### Possible Implementation

See [proof-of-concept on my fork from v10075](https://github.com/uteki-rain/llama.cpp/commit/6b9d07466b8820468510f2650425ed8620797c56).

Notably, the commit involves a subtle bug-fix of `server_tokens::push_back(server_tokens &)` where previously, the token concatenation will throw on a right-hand side with MTMD data because the underlying `server_tokens::push_back(llama_token)` requires the input to not be a `LLAMA_TOKEN_NULL`, which unfortunately is used for padding where MTMD data resides. It also includes a justification of why the `GGML_ASSERT(has_mtmd)` is unnecessary, as part of a comment.

title: Eval bug: vulkan flash attention lets stale K/V in freed cells influence the output
Vulkan: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (GATED_DELTA_NET) decode collapses to ~4 t/s on RDNA4 (gfx1201/RADV) while prefill runs at ~3,200 t/s
body:
### Summary

On a Radeon AI PRO R9700 (Navi 48, `gfx1201`, RADV) with the official **b10331**
`ubuntu-vulkan-x64` release binary, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B decodes at **~3.5 t/s** while the same
weights prefill at **~3,160 t/s** (llama-bench, single stream, no server). A same-class
non-GDN MoE (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, also 3B active) sustains **115.6 t/s** decode on the same
box and build, so this is specific to the GATED_DELTA_NET path, not the machine or the MoE
class.

Serving shows the shape of the failure: generation starts at **~72 t/s for roughly the
first 32 tokens, then falls off a cliff to ~4 t/s** — right at the GDN state-chunk
boundary (64). Quantizing KV to q8_0 makes it worse: **1.72 t/s**.

The magnitude and shape are consistent with the GDN op falling back to CPU (or a
GPU<->CPU state round-trip per layer) in the token-generation path once the recurrent
state chunk fills, while the prompt-processing path stays on the GPU.

### Environment

- llama.cpp **b10331** (commit `7ba604f1c`), official `ubuntu-vulkan-x64` release binary
- GPU: AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 32 GB (Navi 48, RDNA4, `gfx1201`), eGPU over USB4
- Also present: Radeon 890M iGPU (`gfx1150`) — benches pin `GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` (R9700)
- Driver: mesa-vulkan-drivers 25.3.6 (RADV), Fedora 43, kernel 7.1.7-100.fc43.x86_64
- CPU: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (12C/24T), 62 GB RAM
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF` :: `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf`
  (revision `a483e9e6cbd595906af30beda3187c2663a1118c`,
  sha256 `707a55a8a4397ecde44de0c499d3e68c1ad1d240d1da65826b4949d1043f4450`)

### Repro

```
GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 ./llama-bench -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf -fa 1 -ub 2048 -r 3 -o json
```

| test | avg t/s | stddev |
|---|---|---|
| pp512 | 3158.85 | 19.72 |
| tg128 | **3.52** | 0.0004 |

Same command, same box, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-UD-Q4_K_XL (non-GDN A3B MoE control):

| test | avg t/s | stddev |
|---|---|---|
| pp512 | 3524.84 | 44.94 |
| tg128 | **115.55** | 0.07 |

With `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` the 35B decode drops further to **1.72 t/s** (stddev 0.0003).

llama-bench is single-stream and serverless, so this reproduces without any router/parallel
configuration (`llama-server` with a single slot shows the same behavior). The tg128
stddev of 0.0004 shows the slow path is completely deterministic, not thermal/contention
noise.

### Serving-side shape (llama-server, same build/flags as above plus `--jinja`)

- First ~32 generated tokens: ~72 t/s
- After that: ~4 t/s sustained (measured to 2,500+ tokens)
- The knee sits at/near the GDN state-chunk boundary of 64

### Notes

- The Vulkan GATED_DELTA_NET kernels landed in #20334 / #20377 (we pin b8317 as the floor
  for this model family).
- The release tarball ships no `test-backend-ops`, and this box has no compiler toolchain,
  so I could not run `test-backend-ops -o GATED_DELTA_NET` to isolate the op — happy to
  run any diagnostics you want against the release binaries, or build if needed.
- Prefill on the same weights is healthy (3,159 t/s), so weights/quant look fine; only the
  incremental-decode path is affected.

title: [RPC] GET_ROWS can read past an input tensor buffer in release builds
body:
### Name and Version

`ggml-rpc-server` at commit `15586e2d7165` (tag `b10298`), tested on Linux with both ASan and plain RelWithDebInfo builds. Operating system is Linux.

### Affected Module

The ggml RPC backend (`ggml/src/ggml-rpc`) and the CPU `GET_ROWS` kernels.

### Problem description 

I found an out-of-bounds read in the RPC GET_ROWS path. A client can send a GRAPH_COMPUTE request with mismatched input tensor shapes, causing the worker to read past src0 and copy the data into the output tensor, which can then be retrieved with GET_TENSOR.

ggml_get_rows() checks that src0.ne[2] == src1.ne[1], but RPC graph reconstruction bypasses that check. The CPU kernels only enforce the same condition with assert(ne02 == ne11), which is removed when NDEBUG is enabled.

### Reproduce

[rpc_getrows_oob_read.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30884329/rpc_getrows_oob_read.py)

```bash
cmake -B build-rpc-asan -DGGML_RPC=ON -DGGML_SANITIZE_ADDRESS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo \
  -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer" \
```

The RPC server should reject a GET_ROWS graph with incompatible input tensor shapes before running the kernel. Replacing the four assert(ne02 == ne11) checks with GGML_ASSERT prevented the read in my tests. A valid GET_ROWS request still produced the same output after the change. Rejecting the malformed graph at the RPC layer would probably be preferable to aborting the process.

### Scope, AI

I found similar issues in the same RPC backend (GHSA-wcr5-566p-9cwj, GHSA-5vm9-p64x-gqw9, and CVE-2026-34159) that were fixed and assigned despite the RPC disclaimer, so I was not sure whether this case should be considered in scope. I am filing this as a regular issue because SECURITY.md says the RPC backend should not be exposed to untrusted networks. 

I used Claude Code for static analysis and to draft the PoC. I reviewed the relevant code and verified the PoC and test results.

title: Compile bug: KleidiAI .S kernels fail to assemble on Windows ARM64 with llvm-mingw (COFF target) - ELF-only .type/.size in asm preamble
body:
### Git commit

ggml 0.15.2 / commit 5a5a496, KleidiAI v1.24.0 (the version `ggml-cpu/CMakeLists.txt` pins).

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CPU

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Building with `GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON` under **llvm-mingw** on Windows ARM64 fails to assemble every hand-written KleidiAI `.S` micro-kernel, as soon as the arch flags pull those kernels in (anything with `+sve` or `+sme`).

```
cmake -B build -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=<llvm-mingw>/bin/aarch64-w64-mingw32-clang.exe \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=<llvm-mingw>/bin/aarch64-w64-mingw32-clang++.exe \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DGGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF \
  -DGGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH=armv8.2-a+dotprod+i8mm+sve2
cmake --build build
```

`GGML_NATIVE=ON` (the default) hits this too on any CPU whose native detection turns up SVE or SME. On a Snapdragon X2 the configure step reports:

```
-- Adding CPU backend variant ggml-cpu: -mcpu=native+dotprod+i8mm+sve+sme
```

and the build then dies.

**Environment:** llvm-mingw 20260616 UCRT aarch64, target `aarch64-w64-mingw32`, Windows 11 ARM64, Snapdragon X2 Plus.

This is *not* the same as #15653, which is the `arm64-pc-windows-msvc` target and fails at link time with no diagnosis (closed as stale). This one is the GNU-syntax/COFF target, fails at assembly, and has an identified root cause and a verified fix — both below.

### Relevant log output

```shell
kai_matmul_clamp_f32_qsi8d32p4x8_qsi4c32p8x8_16x8_sve_i8mm_asm.S:43:7:
    error: expected absolute expression
kai_matmul_clamp_f32_qsi8d32p4x8_qsi4c32p8x8_16x8_sve_i8mm_asm.S:555:5:
    error: unknown directive

kai_matmul_clamp_f32_qai8dxp1x4_qsi8cxp4vlx4_1x4vl_sme2_dot_asm.S:43:7:
    error: expected absolute expression
kai_matmul_clamp_f32_bf16p2vlx2_bf16p2vlx2_2vlx2vl_sme2_mopa_asm.S:252:5:
    error: unknown directive
```

107 `.S` files are affected — every file carrying the shared macro preamble.

### Root cause

The preamble at the top of each KleidiAI `.S` file branches only two ways:

```c
#if defined(_MSC_VER)
    // ARMASM syntax: GLOBAL / PROC / AREA / DCD / END
#else
    #if defined(__APPLE__)
        #define KAI_ASM_FUNCTION_TYPE(name)                          // Mach-O: correctly empty
        #define KAI_ASM_FUNCTION_END(name)                           // Mach-O: correctly empty
    #else
        #define KAI_ASM_FUNCTION_TYPE(name) .type name, %function    // ELF-only
        #define KAI_ASM_FUNCTION_END(name)  .size name, .-name       // ELF-only
    #endif
#endif
```

The `#else` branch assumes "not MSVC and not Apple" implies ELF. llvm-mingw is a third combination the preamble has no case for: GNU assembler syntax (so the `_MSC_VER` branch is wrong) targeting COFF/PE (so the ELF directives are invalid). `.type` with a `%function` operand and `.size` are both ELF-only, and clang's integrated assembler rejects them for COFF — which is exactly the two errors above, at exactly the `KAI_ASM_FUNCTION_TYPE` and `KAI_ASM_FUNCTION_END` expansion sites.

### Fix

Give Windows the same treatment Mach-O already gets — both macros empty:

```c
    #if defined(__APPLE__) || defined(_WIN32)
        #define KAI_ASM_FUNCTION_TYPE(name)
        #define KAI_ASM_FUNCTION_END(name)
```

`KAI_ASM_GLOBAL` still needs `.global name` without Apple's underscore prefix, so the Windows case can't be folded into the `__APPLE__` branch wholesale — only the `.type`/`.size` pair moves.

I applied this locally by rewriting those two macro definitions across all 107 `.S` files. The build completes, links, runs, and produces byte-identical model output versus the C/intrinsics-only build. The SME kernels are genuinely selected and executed at runtime, not silently skipped:

```
kleidiai: primary q4 kernel feature SME
kleidiai: primary q8 kernel feature SME
kleidiai: SME enabled (runtime-detected SME cores=1)
```

Filing here rather than upstream because https://github.com/ARM-software/kleidiai is a read-only mirror with issues disabled, and the canonical tracker (gitlab.arm.com/kleidi/kleidiai) needs an Arm account. Happy to carry it upstream if that's preferred.

### Impact, and a caveat worth recording

Anyone building with `GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON` on Windows ARM64 via llvm-mingw silently loses every hand-written kernel and gets only the C/intrinsics DOTPROD/I8MM path. With `GGML_NATIVE=ON` the build fails outright on SVE/SME-capable chips instead of degrading.

One caveat so nobody expects a speedup from fixing this: on Snapdragon X2 the SVE/SME kernels turned out **not** to be faster for batch-1 decode. Three interleaved builds, same 30 s clip, byte-identical output, 0.9B model at Q4_K_M:

| build | KleidiAI kernel | median decode |
|---|---|---|
| `+dotprod+i8mm` | I8MM | 6844 ms |
| `+sve2` | I8MM (unchanged) | 10480 ms |
| `+sve2+sme+sme2` | SME | 10477 ms |

SME buys 0.03% — batch-1 decode is memory-bound and a matrix engine adds no memory bandwidth. And `+sve2` costs 53%, because Oryon v3's SVE is 128-bit: `kleidiai.cpp` requires `ggml_cpu_get_sve_cnt() == QK8_0` (256-bit) before it will use its SVE kernels, so all `+sve2` actually changes is that ggml's *own* kernels get compiled to 128-bit SVE for no width gain.

So the build failure is a real bug, but on this CPU the right configuration is `armv8.2-a+dotprod+i8mm` regardless. Other SVE implementations with a 256-bit VL may well see a different answer.

### Compile command

```shell
cmake -B build -G Ninja -DGGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF -DGGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH=armv8.2-a+dotprod+i8mm+sve2
cmake --build build
```

title: Misc. bug: Partial MoE offload (-ncmoe) on integrated GPU is ~2x slower than CPU-only (Arc 140T / Vulkan / UMA)
body:
### Name and Version

./build/bin/llama-cli --version
version: b10335 (74ce157)
built with GNU 16.1.1 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-bench

### Command line

```shell

```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Summary

On a unified-memory system (Intel Arc 140T iGPU, Arrow Lake-H), splitting MoE expert tensors between the Vulkan backend and CPU via `-ncmoe` produces throughput **below both pure-Vulkan and pure-CPU execution**. Since both endpoints share the same physical memory at the same bandwidth, this is not a bandwidth trade-off — the split itself appears to cost more than the GPU contributes.

All measurements below fit entirely in RAM. No disk paging is involved.

### Hardware / software

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | Intel Core Ultra 9 285H (6 P + 8 E + 2 LP-E) |
| iGPU | Intel Arc 140T (Xe-LPG+, gfx 12.74.4), `uma: 1`, `matrix cores: none` |
| RAM | 32 GB LPDDR5x-8533 (~136 GB/s theoretical) |
| OS | Arch Linux, KDE Plasma 6 |
| Driver | Mesa ANV (open-source) |
| Build | `74ce157`, `-DGGML_VULKAN=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` |
| Model | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M (`ggml-org/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF`), 19.01 GiB, 40 layers, 3B active |

### Results

```
llama-bench -hf ggml-org/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF:Q4_K_M -p 512 -n 128 -t 4 [+ variant flag]
```

| config | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) |
|---|---|---|
| Vulkan, all layers on GPU (default) | 249.17 ± 1.19 | **18.49 ± 0.18** |
| CPU only (`-dev none`) | 54.13 ± 2.39 | **12.19 ± 0.18** |
| Split (`-ncmoe 40`) | 80.80 ± 8.49 | **5.68 ± 0.17** |

The split configuration is **2.15x slower than CPU-only**, despite the CPU doing strictly *less* work in the split case (experts only, vs. the entire model in `-dev none`).

### Scaling with number of offloaded blocks

`-t 4`, varying `-ncmoe`:

| `-ncmoe` | tg128 (t/s) | ms/token |
|---|---|---|
| 0  | 18.13 ± 0.21 | 55.2 |
| 10 | 10.30 ± 1.22 | 97.1 |
| 20 | 8.18 ± 0.93  | 122.2 |
| 30 | 8.47 ± 0.33  | 118.1 |
| 40 | 5.68 ± 0.17  | 176.1 |

Latency grows roughly linearly with the number of offloaded blocks (~3 ms per block), which is consistent with a fixed per-block cost rather than a bandwidth effect. Run-to-run variance is also much higher in split configs (±1.22 at `-ncmoe 10` vs ±0.18 elsewhere).

### Thread scaling under split

Thread count does not recover the loss; more threads make it worse.

| threads | tg128, `-ncmoe 40` | tg128, `-ncmoe 0` |
|---|---|---|
| 2  | 5.53 ± 0.08 | — |
| 4  | 5.91 ± 0.18 | 18.49 ± 0.18 |
| 6  | 5.41 ± 0.13 | — |
| 8  | 5.50 ± 0.23 | 18.52 ± 0.07 |
| 12 | 4.82 ± 0.10 | 18.69 ± 0.18 |
| 16 | 4.47 ± 0.04 | 18.62 ± 0.10 |

At `-ncmoe 0` the flat curve indicates a memory-bound workload. Under split, 2 threads already reach 94% of peak — the CPU compute is not the limiting factor either.

### Why this seems anomalous

On a UMA system the CPU and iGPU read the same DRAM at the same bandwidth, so a split should degrade toward the slower endpoint, not below both. The per-block linearity and insensitivity to thread count both point at fixed per-boundary overhead (graph split synchronisation / command buffer submission) rather than compute or bandwidth.

I have not root-caused this — the above is inference from the scaling behaviour, not from profiling. Happy to run `GGML_VULKAN_PERF_LOGGER=1` or any other instrumentation on request.

### Practical impact

Standard guidance is to offload whatever fits and leave the rest on CPU. On this hardware that guidance is inverted: for any model where full GPU residency isn't possible, `-dev none` outperforms partial offload by ~2x. This likely affects other UMA platforms (Intel iGPUs, AMD APUs, Snapdragon X) where the same assumption doesn't hold.

### Not the issue (already ruled out)

- **Load mode**: `-lm mmap` vs `-lm dio` — no meaningful difference (18.51 vs 18.80).
- **Cooperative matrix**: Mesa exposes `VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix` with `cooperativeMatrix = true` but advertises no shapes. Force-enabling coopmat for the Mesa driver ID produces a 2.7–3.3x regression (dense 3B: 681 → 255 pp512; this MoE model: 249 → 82 pp512), confirming the existing `eIntelProprietaryWindows` restriction in `ggml_vk_khr_cooperative_matrix_support()` is correct for this driver.
- **SYCL backend**: builds and runs correctly (oneDNN linked, `GGML_SYCL_DNNL: yes`, Level Zero enumerates the GPU) but is slower than Vulkan on this hardware in every configuration tested — dense 3B: 383 vs 681 pp512, 23.0 vs 32.6 tg128.

<summary>Logs</summary>

title: Eval bug: Image prompt cache never hits for hybrid SSM models (Qwen3.6) when only the text suffix changes
body:
### Name and Version

version: 0.1.0-dev (build 73, commit 8e7f22b67)
built with AppleClang 17.0.0.17000013 for Darwin arm64

### Operating systems

Linux, Mac, Windows

### GGML backends

Metal, CUDA

### Hardware

Apple M1 Max
(the issue is not HW specific)

### Models

Qwen3.6 (both the 27B dense and the 35B MoE)
One of my tests: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL + mmproj-F16.


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

**Use case**: I send several queries against the same image, changing only the text that follows it: [image][text query 1], then [image][text query 2], and so on. The image is byte-identical and is the prefix. 
Not image-specific. Can be reproduced on tools/mtmd/test-1.jpeg

**Expected**: I expect the image prefix to be encoded only once.

**Actual**: On the Qwen3.6 series (qwen35, qwen35moe) every request re-encodes the image prefix.

This works as expected on Qwen3-VL (non hybrid), 

Qwen3.6 is hybrid attention + SSM, so the memory is recurrent and cannot roll back to an arbitrary position. The LCP is found, then discarded: see the **Log 1** below.

I thought that checkpoints can still save my usecase, but negative, they also fail: see the **Log 2** below.
The first checkpoint happens in the middle of the text prompt, and that part is changing in my usecase.
In my test the rejection is the first clause of the search predicate at `server-context.cpp:3364`,
```cpp
if (cur.pos_max > pos_next) return false;
```
The checkpoint lands at position 128; the divergence is at position 115. 

Ideally the checkpoint should be recorded immediately after the image. But that is prohibited in code `server-context.cpp:3615`,
```cpp
// do not checkpoint after mtmd chunks
do_checkpoint = do_checkpoint && !has_mtmd;
```

I could not find the particular reason the guard is there. And I confirmed that removing it fixes my usecase.
Before I go ahead and suggest a PR, I'd like to ask the maintainers about this. Perhaps, @ggerganov still remembers and can comment?

There is a couple of relevant commits that I've found:
ab9d4c367 improve mtmd ctx checkpoints (#20726) - introduced the guard with no stated reason;
5d9e5ac30 support slot save/restore with media inputs (#26640) -  later added media serialization to slot state and did not revisit it.

title: SYCL: MoE expert tensors never get the Q8_0 reorder path (opt_for_reorder_id)
body:
*Note up front: I used an AI assistant to read through the SYCL source and to parse the tensor tables out of the GGUF files, and to help me write this up. The measurements are from my own machine and I checked them myself. Flagging it so you know what you're reading.*

## What I ran into

I'm running Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (MoE, 40 layers, 256 experts, 8 active) on an Arc Pro B50 16GB, SYCL backend, build b10499. Because the model doesn't fit in VRAM I offload part of the experts to CPU with `-ncmoe`, so I care a lot about which tensors get the reorder treatment.

While figuring out which quant to use, I found that reorder coverage does not go up as the quant gets bigger. It peaks at Q4_K and then falls off a cliff.

The reason is that the MoE path has a narrower type gate than the dense path — [`opt_for_reorder_id`, ggml-sycl.cpp#L4458-L4472](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/9a286ac98d2cab74231bd3f1fc3f2b8bdf05422e/ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp#L4458-L4472) (pinned at master `9a286ac`):

```c
static void opt_for_reorder_id(ggml_backend_sycl_context * ctx, const ggml_tensor * src0) {
    ...
    if (src0->type != GGML_TYPE_Q4_K && src0->type != GGML_TYPE_Q5_K && src0->type != GGML_TYPE_Q6_K) {
        return;
    }
```

The dense gates (`ggml_sycl_supports_reorder_dmmv` / `_mmvq`) also accept Q1_0, Q4_0, Q8_0, Q2_K and Q3_K. The MoE gate takes three types only.

This isn't a correctness problem — output is fine. It's just that a large part of the model silently skips the optimization.

## Why it matters on a real model

On a 35B-A3B, the expert tensors are around 85-90% of the file. So whatever the expert gate rejects is most of the model.

Unsloth's Dynamic quants promote expert tensors to Q8_0 at the higher tiers, and Q8_0 isn't on that list. I measured coverage by reading the tensor types straight out of each GGUF and weighting by bytes (expert tensors judged against `opt_for_reorder_id`, everything else against the dense gates):

| file | expert tensor types | reorder coverage |
|---|---|--:|
| UD-Q4_K_S | Q4_K 18.1G, Q6_K 0.7G | ~100% |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | Q4_K 12.1G, Q5_K 7.4G, Q6_K 0.7G | ~100% |
| UD-Q5_K_XL | Q5_K 14.8G, Q6_K 8.8G, Q8_0 0.9G | 96% |
| UD-Q6_K_XL | Q6_K 17.6G, **Q8_0 12.3G** | **62%** |
| UD-Q8_K_XL | **Q8_0 33.7G** | **7%** |

(files from `peculiar-ragdoll/Nail-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF-MTP`, which redistributes Unsloth's quants)

So on Intel, paying for Q6_K_XL gets you worse throughput than Q4_K_XL, on a file that is 10GB larger. Nothing in the filename hints at that, and there's no warning at load time.

I can't give you a clean before/after for Q8_0 experts specifically, since the code path doesn't exist to turn on. What I can say is that reorder on the expert path is clearly worth a lot on this hardware: UD-Q4_K_S (~100% covered) with 20 layers of experts spilled to CPU still beats UD-IQ3_XXS (0% expert coverage, IQ types aren't eligible anywhere) running entirely in VRAM — 42.8 t/s vs 35.9 t/s, despite being 8GB bigger and partly on DDR4. Different quant types so it's not a controlled comparison, but the gap is large enough that I don't think it's noise.

## The groundwork already landed

Q8_0 reorder exists for dense tensors — #21527 added `reorder_qw_q8_0` plus DMMV/MMVQ dispatch back in April, and it's a nice win there (3.1x reported).

The MoE variants exist too, just not for Q8_0. Current kernel list:

```
reorder_qw_q4_0     reorder_qw_q4_k     reorder_qw_q4_k_moe
reorder_qw_q8_0     reorder_qw_q5_k     reorder_qw_q5_k_moe
reorder_qw_q2_k     reorder_qw_q6_k     reorder_qw_q6_k_moe
reorder_qw_q3_k                         <- no q8_0_moe
```

From the outside it looks like the missing pieces are a `reorder_qw_q8_0_moe` alongside the three that are already there, and adding `GGML_TYPE_Q8_0` to the gate above. I haven't written or tested that, so I may well be underestimating it — the `_moe` variants handle the per-expert stride and I don't know how much of that carries over.

Q2_K, Q3_K and Q4_0 are in the same position (accepted on dense, rejected for experts), but Q8_0 is the one that actually shows up in expert tensors in the quants people download, so it seemed like the one worth raising.

## To reproduce

No special setup — the gate is visible in the source. To see the effect on a real file, read the tensor types from any Unsloth UD MoE quant at Q6_K or above and check how many bytes of `ffn_*_exps.weight` are Q8_0.

## Offering to test

I have an Arc Pro B50 (Battlemage, 16GB) and a set of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B quants from IQ3 up to Q6_K already benchmarked on it, with a repeatable harness (warmed runs, greedy sampling, fixed 25k-token prompt). If someone puts up a patch I'm happy to run it and report numbers, including the partial-offload case which is probably the interesting one.

Environment:
- Intel Arc Pro B50 16GB (Battlemage, `xe` driver)
- Ryzen 5 5600GT, 30GB DDR4, no swap
- llama.cpp b10499, SYCL AOT build
- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE, 128k context, `--spec-type draft-mtp`
